newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Suez turned Israeli doubts into self-confidence.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Suez turned Israeli doubts into self-confidence.

text.p: Britain and France emerged from the Suez crisis as end-of-empire losers, but Israel came out a winner on the path to becoming a Middle East nuclear power.
Forty years ago this month Britain and France, secretly in league with Israel, failed to retake the Suez Canal from Egypt.
"On the other hand Israel came out with very solid gains," Abba Eban, who was Israel's U.S. and U.N. ambassador at the time, told Reuters.
The Israelis crossed the Gaza Strip and Sinai Desert with the declared aim of stopping attacks by Egyptian-backed Palestinian fedayeen guerrillas.

They managed to pry open the Straits of Tiran, a crucial Red Sea trade route to Asia and Africa which had been closed by Egypt. The opening of the Straits enabled Israel to turn its desolate southernmost point into a thriving port -- Eilat.
For Israeli prime minister David Ben-Gurion, this was most important.

"Ben-Gurion made a list of what would be the priorities from the point of view of Israel and the highest priority...was the opening of the Straits of Tiran and that was what we got," said Yuval Ne'eman, 71, who was deputy head of military intelligence.
Despite charges that Israel had collaborated with imperialists, its influence grew in newly developing Africa and Asia.
"It did not have the negative effects in the Third World that had been expected...I think it was a direct result of our military success," said Eban, now 81.
Trade expanded and Iranian oil flowed through Israel to European markets.
When months later Israel's troops pulled out, the United Nations created a force in Gaza and Sinai that kept southern Israel tranquil until the next war in 1967.

"There was so much tranquility that when President (Gamal Abdel) Nasser began his troop movements in 1967 the Israeli forces were totally concentrated on the Syrian and Jordanian fronts and time was needed to bring our forces down," Eban said.
The conflict was the first big test of Israel's military mettle since its War of Independence in 1948. After years of fighting alone, Israel felt euphoric having partners.

"Ben-Gurion told me...he had been very reluctant to start any kind of military operation without having a great power behind him," Ne'eman, a physics professor and former cabinet minister in right-wing Likud-led governments, told Reuters.
"His lesson from the War of Independence had been that there were very hard moments when there was nobody behind Israel and Israel was at the mercy of pressures and ultimatums," he said.
The French connection in the operation was by all accounts crucial for one big reason.

Shimon Peres, who as director-general of Israel's Defence Ministry helped negotiate the secret deal, won agreement for France to build Israel's nuclear reactor at Dimona in southern Israel and supply the natural uranium to fuel it.

"The close alliance with France made it possible to purchase a nuclear reactor," said Ne'eman, who like Peres, was active in the Dimona project which is widely seen as the seed of Israel's nuclear arsenal.
The week that began on October 29, 1956, was trying for both the Israeli military and its diplomacy.
Israel lost 171 men and Egypt several thousand.
At one point the Soviet Union threatened to intervene on Egypt's behalf and for the first time Israel seemed threatened with liquidation by a power capable of destroying it.
When Ben-Gurion hinted in parliament he was thinking of annexing parts of Sinai, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower warned him not to count on American help should Israel face a Soviet-assisted attack.
By March 1957 Israel was out of Sinai and Gaza, replaced by a U.N. emergency force.

Eban said the conflict arose from Israel's perception that it was losing its deterrent power to a Soviet-backed Egypt. It taught the U.S the importance of Israel's maintaining deterrent power, he said.

"Israel had much more military confidence after that...and the United States, in spite of having opposed the Israeli initiative in war, reached the conclusion that it was wrong to leave Israel alone or to isolate Israel because this would have explosive results," Eban said.

"It was from that date onwards that we find the United States helping Israel to acquire jet aircraft," he said. Today Israel is the biggest recipient of U.S. aid at $3 billion a year -- $1.8 billion in military aid.
The 1956 experience still makes headlines in Israel, even if they're not the sort the country would like.

Last year a retired Israeli army officer said he had killed 49 Egyptian prisoners-of-war during the crisis. Although pressed by Egypt to act, Israel's attorney-general said a 20-year statute of limitations had expired.
Palestinians jumped on the disclosure, however, alleging Israel also carried out a massacre in Gaza. Israel promised to investigate.
